stories.title: From Gallion to the Statewide Stage: Dr. Valencia Wells Makes History in Optometry
stories.summary: Dr. Valencia Wells wrote a research paper on optometry in eighth grade. More than two decades later, she's the first Black person — male or female — to serve as president of the 125-year-old Alabama Optometric Association.
stories.extended_summary: In eighth grade, growing up in rural Gallion, Alabama, Valencia Wells wrote a research paper on optometry. She'd worn glasses since second grade and admired her own eye doctor. Dentistry was out. Pharmacy didn't appeal. Physical therapy was off the table due to her scoliosis surgery. Optometry stuck. More than two decades later, Dr. Wells owns Morris Avenue Eyecare, mentors young professionals, and has just become the first Black person — male or female — to serve as president of the Alabama Optometric Association in its 125-year history. 'It represents not only a personal achievement,' she said, 'but a milestone for representation and progress.'

stories.title: High schooler honored at surprise ceremony for saving father from cardiac arrest
stories.summary: Jackson Suarez found his father on the ground, not breathing. He started CPR — and saved his dad's life. Now his school is honoring him with a surprise ceremony, and his mom wants every kid to learn CPR.
stories.extended_summary: "He was on the ground like a starfish. His eyes were open but they weren't looking at me. So I started CPR." Those are the words of Jackson Suarez, a high schooler who saved his own father's life in July. Hector Suarez doesn't remember any of it — he just dropped. Thanks to CPR skills Jackson learned through a school program, Hector was alive to attend the surprise ceremony honoring his son. Jackson's teacher presented him with a plaque of his father's heart rhythm. His mom now hopes the rescue pushes every school to teach CPR. "Without it," she says, "his dad wouldn't have been here."

stories.title: Monk-inspired 20-second reset found to be a key to well-being. But it must be done daily.
stories.summary: A Harvard psychologist spent a month at Thich Nhat Hanh's Plum Village and learned that three breaths — not three hours — might be the real key to mindfulness. His research backs a 20-second daily reset that actually works.
stories.extended_summary: Psychologist Eli Susman went to Plum Village, Thich Nhat Hanh's mindfulness center, and meditated for three hours in his room — expecting praise. A monk's response changed everything: 'How about three breaths? That's all you need to tune into the present moment.' Humbled, Susman began researching whether short, daily mindfulness practices could deliver real benefits. His work at Harvard and UC Berkeley led to a research-backed 20-second reset that, done consistently, measurably improves well-being. The finding challenges the assumption that mindfulness requires long sessions or retreats — sometimes the smallest daily habit is the one that sticks.

stories.summary: Casey Baker-Romans designed a vape disposal program that's now in over two dozen Kentucky schools, preventing nearly 6.7 million puffs of nicotine and THC exposure. Her work just earned her a spot in the 2026 class of Healthy Kentucky Champions.
stories.extended_summary: Nearly 6.7 million puffs of nicotine and THC never reached Kentucky students — because one health educator built a vape disposal program that now runs in more than two dozen schools. This week she was named to the 2026 class of Healthy Kentucky Champions, making her a finalist for a $5,000 grant she'd direct to a Kentucky nonprofit. stories.title: Renovated CARITAS men’s campus puts dignity at the center of recovery
stories.summary: Cameron Patey once tended bar while battling addiction. Now, at CARITAS' newly renovated men's campus in Richmond, he helps other men walk the same recovery path he did — and the program served 380 men last year.
stories.extended_summary: Cameron Patey used to pour drinks behind a bar. Now the 29-year-old walks the halls of CARITAS' freshly renovated men's campus in Richmond's Southside, guiding other men through The Healing Place — the same long-term residential recovery program that changed his own life. When he first walked through those doors in 2025, he wasn't sure he was ready. "I had never undergone any treatment," he says. "Never thought about recovery." What he found was structure: months of classes, a 12-step foundation, and food, clothing, and medical care, all free. The program served 380 men last year. Patey's life looks different now — built, he says, on a deep dedication to sobriety.

stories.summary: Mercury Stardust — the Trans Handy Ma'am — taught 4.8 million followers how to fix their homes. Now she's touring with her second book, bringing live storytelling and trans folk-punk to Cleveland, because home, she says, is everything.
stories.extended_summary: More than 4.8 million people know Mercury Stardust as the Trans Handy Ma'am — the burlesque performer turned home repair technician whose TikTok tutorials taught a generation of renters and LGBTQ+ folks how to fix a leaky faucet and hang a shelf. Her first book hit #1 on the New York Times bestseller list. Now she's on tour for her second, "Lost and Found: A Compassionate Guide to Homeownership," with a stop at Cleveland's No Class on Oct. 12 featuring live music from trans folk-punk artist House of Wills. "Home is not just drywall and electrical and plumbing," Stardust says. "Home is where the people you love are."

stories.title: Utah tech leader reflects on his dual HR role and modernization
stories.summary: Brock Arnold already ran HR for Roosevelt, Utah — then the IT manager job opened up and he took it too. He moved the city's antiquated systems to the cloud, cutting a three-day payroll process down to almost nothing.
stories.extended_summary: Roosevelt, Utah has about 7,000 residents, so when the IT manager job opened up, the guy already running HR just took it. "I joke with people that the reason I'm over at IT is because I'm the person who knows the most about it," Brock Arnold says. He inherited systems he calls "antiquated" and moved the city onto a cloud platform — payroll for 51 full-time and 180 part-time employees used to take three days and required supervisors to come in on Sunday afternoons to approve payments. Now it doesn't. In small-town government, one person wearing two hats can modernize an entire city.

stories.title: What It Takes to Have a Friday Night Without Violence
stories.summary: In South Memphis, a violence intervention team called Heal 901 threw a Family Fun Friday — carnival rides, food trucks, goats to pet — to give families a safe place to be together. Their real work is interrupting cycles of conflict, but some nights it's just joy.
stories.extended_summary: On a Friday night in July, Martin Luther King Jr. Park in South Memphis had carnival rides, food trucks, goats to pet, and a young woman airbrushing "901" onto a kid's forearm. Moving through the crowd: anti-violence workers in bright orange shirts reading "END COMMUNITY VIOLENCE." They're from Heal 901, a small violence intervention team whose community safety specialists help people navigate cycles of conflict and the justice system. Their work is complex and often invisible. But that night, their job was simpler — give families a safe place to spend an evening together. "It brings joy. It brings fun. It brings a sense of belonging," said one organizer.

stories.title: When It Pays for an Agency to Break the Rules
stories.summary: Chris Crawford was told to launch his ad agency on Madison Avenue. Instead he started it in a one-bedroom Harlem apartment, invested in a step-show platform, sold it to Sony, and built a business around ethics and community — landing clients like the U.S. Army.
stories.extended_summary: Everyone told Chris Crawford he needed a Madison Avenue address and a Rolodex full of new business leads. He launched Elite Media in a one-bedroom apartment in Harlem instead, betting on the clients he already had. "There's no way you can super-service a partner if you're constantly thinking about all the other people you can connect to," he says. He put his own money into Stomp the Yard, reimagining college step shows as WWE-level national championships — and sold the platform to Sony. That payday moved him out of his mother's house and attracted clients like the U.S. Army and Boost Mobile. His model: ethics, equity, and community, in an industry that rarely rewards any of the three.

stories.title: ‘I love telling people that I’m a mechanic’: This Gen Z woman ditched her law aspirations for blue-collar work—and now outearns her friends
stories.summary: Victoria Madsen was studying English and planning for law school. Now she's a lift mechanic at Sundance Mountain Resort — and outearning her friends. Nearly half of Gen Z is considering the trades, and she's proof it pays.
stories.extended_summary: Victoria Madsen wanted to be a lawyer. She was studying English at Utah Valley when she pivoted — and now, at 25, she runs the ski lifts at Sundance Mountain Resort, starting up the machinery at dawn on the slopes of Mount Timpanogos. "I'm really proud of the job that I have," she says. "I love telling people that I'm a mechanic." She outearns her friends. She's part of a wave: nearly half of Americans ages 16 to 30 are learning a trade or seriously considering one, and 30 percent say AI anxiety pushed them toward blue-collar work. Ford's CEO says Gen Z needs its own "Smokey Bear moment" for the trades. Madsen already had hers.
